title: Thirsting for the Living God
sum: Psalm 42 (Greek 41) opens Book II of the Psalter and the collection of the sons of Korah. A worshiper far from the temple, in the north near the springs of the Jordan and Mount Hermon, compares himself to a deer at a dry stream bed. He remembers leading the festival crowds up to the house of God; now his tears are his bread, and people mock him: "Where is your God?" Twice he argues with his own soul: "Why are you so bowed down?... Wait for God."

Psalm 42 and Psalm 43 are almost certainly one poem in three stanzas, each ending with the same refrain (42:5, 42:11, 43:5). The first stanza remembers worship, the second feels God's own waves rolling over the speaker, and the third (Psalm 43) prays to be led back to the altar. This psalm also begins the "Elohistic Psalter" (42–83), where "God" largely replaces the name "the LORD."
readings: Read as an exile's prayer

Many hear a Judean carried off to the north, or a priest or singer cut off from Jerusalem in a time of exile, longing for the temple and mocked by foreigners (43:1). The geography of 42:6 suits a journey out of the land.
Read as every believer's dark night

From Augustine to modern writers on depression, readers have taken the psalm as the prayer of anyone who feels God's absence, and the refrain as a pattern for speaking honestly to one's own despair while still holding on to hope.

views.H: The title gives no occasion. Some traditional interpreters linked it with David's flight across the Jordan from Absalom (2 Samuel 17:22–24), but the title names the sons of Korah, not David.
views.C: An individual lament, joined with Psalm 43 into one poem. Most date it to the monarchy or the exile; Goulder argued that the Korah psalms come from the northern sanctuary at Dan, near the Jordan's sources, which would explain the setting of 42:6.
views.L: In the old Roman rite, Psalm 42 (the tract Sicut cervus, Latin 41:2–4) was sung at the Easter Vigil as the procession went to the font for the baptisms, and Psalm 43 opened nearly every Mass. The present Roman Easter Vigil uses Psalms 42–43 as the responsorial psalm when baptism is celebrated. Palestrina's Sicut cervus and the English hymn "As pants the hart" (Tate and Brady, 1696) are settings.
views.J: The Midrash on Psalms compares Israel to the deer that cries out to God. Rashi reads the stanzas as the voice of Israel in exile remembering the temple.
views.X: Augustine preached that the deer kills snakes and then thirsts: the soul that puts its sins to death thirsts for God. Christians have read 42:2 as longing for the vision of God (Matthew 5:8; 1 Corinthians 13:12) and the living water Christ gives (John 7:37–38).

deep.h: Psalms 42 and 43: one poem or two?
deep.b:
Four facts suggest one poem. Psalm 43 has no title, which is very unusual in Book II. The refrain of 42:5 and 42:11 returns as 43:5. 43:2 repeats 42:9 almost word for word ("Why must I go about in black, / with the enemy pressing me?"). And a number of medieval Hebrew manuscripts copy the two as a single psalm. Read together, the poem has three stanzas of about the same length. The first remembers the festival crowd (42:1–5); the second is drowning in God's waves (42:6–11); the third asks for light and faithfulness to lead the speaker home, and promises praise at the altar (43:1–5). The movement is from memory, through the depths, to hope.

Why then were they divided? Perhaps for use in worship, where Psalm 43 could stand alone as a prayer of approach to the altar, as it did for centuries in the Latin Mass. The Greek translation already divides them and gives Psalm 43 a title ("A psalm of David"), which shows the division is old. This site follows the standard numbering, but the notes and chapter pages treat 42–43 as one poem.

echoes: Psalm 43:1–5; Psalm 63:1; Psalm 84:1–2; Psalm 143:6; Joel 1:20; Jonah 2:3; Psalm 79:10; Psalm 115:2; John 4:10; John 7:37–38; Revelation 22:17

settings.what: A lament of a worshiper far from the temple (first two stanzas of 42–43)
settings.by: an unnamed singer of the Korahite guild (the title); perhaps a Levite who once led festival processions (42:4)
settings.to: God (42:1, 42:6–9), his own soul (42:5, 42:11) and, by overhearing, the congregation
settings.when: far from Jerusalem, in the north near the Jordan's springs (42:6), while mocked by enemies who ask "Where is your God?" (42:3, 42:10)
settings.why: to pour out grief at God's absence without giving up on him, and to talk the despairing self back to hope. Knowing the speaker once led worship explains why exclusion from the temple feels like thirst and drowning.
settings.readers: For Israelites after the exile praying the collected Psalter, many of whom lived far from Jerusalem, the psalm gave words for longing for the temple and for answering the nations' mockery with stubborn hope.
views: An exile on the way to, or living in, a foreign land (Rashi; many modern scholars).
A northern Israelite at Dan or near Hermon, cut off from Zion (Goulder).
A sick or persecuted Levite barred from the temple; the geography is figurative.

title: Send Your Light
sum: Psalm 43 (Greek 42) has no title and finishes the poem begun in Psalm 42. The speaker asks God to take up his case against a faithless nation and a deceitful man, asks again why God has pushed him away, and then turns to a clear request: send your light and your faithfulness to guide me back to your holy mountain. There he will go up to the altar and praise God on the lyre. The refrain closes the whole poem for the third time.

This short prayer of approach to the altar had a long life of its own: from 1570 to 1970 nearly every Roman Catholic Mass began with it (Requiems and Masses of Passiontide left it out), the priest and server saying it at the foot of the altar.

views.H: Traditional readers who give Psalm 42 to the Korahites give this part to them as well. The Greek title, "A psalm of David," reflects an early wish to give every psalm an author.
views.C: The closing stanza of the lament of 42–43, with the move from complaint to confident request typical of the genre (Gunkel).
views.L: As Iudica me, Psalm 43 (Latin 42) formed the prayers at the foot of the altar in the Tridentine Mass. It was dropped in the 1970 Missal but is still prayed in the traditional Latin Mass.
views.J: Rashi reads "a nation without loyalty" as the nations who exiled Israel. Midrash Tehillim reads "your light and your truth" as the two redeemers of the end, Elijah and the Messiah (Malachi 4:5; Isaiah 42:1), as Moses and Aaron were sent to Egypt.
views.X: Christian writers took the light and truth of 43:3 as Christ, "the light of the world" and "the truth" (John 8:12; John 14:6), who leads the soul to the altar of God.

echoes: Psalm 42:5; Psalm 42:9; Psalm 42:11; Psalm 26:1; Psalm 27:1; Psalm 36:9; Psalm 84:1; John 8:12; John 14:6

settings.what: The closing stanza of the lament of Psalms 42–43
settings.when: still far from the temple, opposed by a faithless people and a deceitful man (43:1)
settings.why: to ask God to defend him and to lead him back to worship, and to promise the thanksgiving he will bring at the altar. The request turns the despair of Psalm 42 into a concrete hope: a road home.
settings.readers: After the exile, worshipers who prayed the poem at the rebuilt temple could hear their own return in "they will bring me to your holy mountain."

title: Why Do You Sleep, Lord?
sum: Psalm 44 (Greek 43) is a lament of the whole nation after a military defeat. It begins with the old stories: God, not Israel's sword, planted the ancestors in the land. Then comes the shock: God has rejected his people, sent them out without him, sold them cheap and scattered them, and made them a joke among the nations. The people insist they have not forgotten God or broken his covenant. It is for his sake that they are killed all day long.

The ending is one of the boldest prayers in the Bible: "Get up! Why do you sleep, Lord?" The psalm does not explain the suffering as punishment. Paul quotes 44:22 in Romans 8:36 to describe Christians who suffer for belonging to God.
readings: Read as protest
The psalm stands with Job and Psalms 73 and 89 as a faithful protest: Israel will not accept that its suffering is deserved, and says so to God. Faith here takes the form of argument.
Read as martyrdom
Jewish and Christian readers have heard in 44:22 the voice of those who die because of their faith: the Maccabean martyrs, the victims of persecution in every age, and, for Paul, the church.

views.H: Titled only "Of the sons of Korah." Some traditional interpreters placed it in David's wars with Edom (compare the title of Psalm 60) or in Hezekiah's time.
views.C: A community lament. Proposed settings run from the late monarchy (701 or 586 BC) to the Maccabean period. The claim of national innocence fits best with a time of loyalty, such as after Josiah's reform, or a persecution for faith.
views.L: Recited in times of national disaster in both synagogue and church.
views.J: The Talmud tells that the Levites called "the wakers" sang 44:23 daily in the temple until John Hyrcanus stopped it (Mishnah Sotah 9:10; Bavli Sotah 48a). Bavli Gittin 57b applies 44:22 to the mother and her seven sons who died rather than worship an idol, and the verse became a classic text for kiddush hashem, dying for the sanctification of God's name.
views.X: Romans 8:35–37 quotes 44:22 and answers it: nothing can separate believers from God's love in Christ. Calvin read the psalm as a prayer for the church under persecution and dated it to the Maccabees.

deep.b: Most of the Old Testament teaches that Israel's disasters come from its sins: Deuteronomy 28, Judges 2, 2 Kings 17. Psalm 44 knows that pattern and denies that it applies: "All this came on us, / yet we did not forget you" (44:17). The people ask God to search their hearts (44:21), confident of what he will find. Scholars have called it the Old Testament's sharpest challenge to the rule of reward and punishment, alongside Job. The psalm does not resolve the problem. It simply holds two things together, that God is the one who acts in history (44:1–8) and that God has let his loyal people be crushed (44:9–22), and it appeals to his loyal love (44:26). Paul's use in Romans 8 gives one Christian answer: such suffering is the mark of belonging to God, not of being abandoned by him.

echoes: Romans 8:35–37; Joshua 24:12; Deuteronomy 8:17–18; Deuteronomy 28:37; Psalm 74:1–23; Psalm 79:1–13; Psalm 89:38–51; Isaiah 51:9; Mark 4:38; 2 Maccabees 7:1–41

settings.by: the people of Israel, with a leader, perhaps the king, speaking as "I" (44:4, 44:6, 44:15)
settings.when: after a lost war, with the people scattered and mocked by their neighbors (44:10–14); probably at a public fast at the temple (compare Joel 2:15–17)
settings.why: to remind God of his past acts, to protest that the defeat is not deserved, and to call him to wake up and redeem them for his loyal love's sake. Knowing it is the whole nation speaking makes the claim of innocence a claim of covenant loyalty, not of sinless individuals.
settings.readers: For the community after the exile, still under foreign rule, the psalm gave a way to keep faith when history seemed to contradict God's promises.
views: A defeat under a king of Judah, such as in 701 BC or under Josiah (Kraus).
The fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC.
The persecution under Antiochus IV, when Jews died for refusing idolatry (Calvin, Theodore of Mopsuestia); most scholars think this too late for the Psalter's formation.

title: Your Throne, O God
sum: Psalm 45 (Greek 44) is the only wedding song in the Psalter. A court poet sings in praise of the king on his wedding day: his beauty and grace, his sword and victories for truth and justice, his throne and scepter, his anointing "with the oil of joy," his perfumed robes and ivory palaces. Then he turns to the bride, a foreign princess: forget your people, the king desires your beauty. She is led in, splendid in gold, with her companions. The poem ends with a promise of sons and an everlasting name.

Its most famous line is 45:6, "Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever," which Hebrews 1:8–9 quotes of the Son of God. The Targum calls the king "King Messiah," and Jews and Christians alike have read the psalm as a picture of the Messiah and his bride.
readings: Read as a royal wedding
The first meaning: a song performed at the marriage of a king of Israel or Judah to a foreign princess, praising the king as the ideal ruler and urging the bride to embrace her new home.
Read as Messiah and bride
From the Targum and Hebrews to the church fathers and the Song of Songs tradition, the king is the Messiah and the bride is Israel, the church or (in Catholic and Orthodox devotion) Mary.

views.H: The title names the sons of Korah, not the king. Traditional proposals for the occasion include Solomon's marriage to Pharaoh's daughter (1 Kings 3:1) or to another foreign princess.
views.C: A royal psalm from the monarchy. Some suggest the northern kingdom, for example Ahab's marriage to Jezebel of Sidon (1 Kings 16:31), since Tyre is named and ivory palaces are known from Samaria; others prefer a Judean king. It was kept after the monarchy ended because it was read of the hoped-for king.
views.L: Sung in the church on feasts of Christ and of Mary (Latin Eructavit cor meum), and on Christmas.
views.J: The Targum: "Your beauty, O King Messiah, is greater than the sons of men." Rashi reads the psalm of Torah scholars; Ibn Ezra of David or the Messiah. The Talmud uses 45:13 to praise the modesty of the king's daughter "inside" (Bavli Yevamot 77a).
views.X: Hebrews 1:8–9 quotes 45:6–7 to show that the Son is addressed as God and anointed above his companions. The fathers read the bride as the church (Augustine) and the queen at the right hand as Mary, especially in the East; Origen and Bernard linked the psalm with the Song of Songs.

deep.h: "Your throne, O God" (45:6): the Hebrew, the versions and Hebrews
deep.b:
The Hebrew. The line reads kis'akha elohim 'olam va'ed, "your throne / God / forever and ever," with no verb. The king has been addressed as "you" since 45:2, so kis'akha is the king's throne. The question is how elohim stands in the sentence.

Reading 1: vocative, "Your throne, O God." This is the most natural grammar, and the Masoretic accents treat elohim as a separate word of address. The Greek (ho thronos sou ho theos), Jerome's two Latin Psalters (thronus tuus Deus; sedes tua Deus) and Hebrews 1:8 all read it this way, as do the KJV, NRSV and most modern versions. If the king is called elohim, it can be read in at least three ways: (a) as royal language, the king as God's representative, the way elohim is used of rulers or judges (Exodus 21:6; 82:6) and Moses is made "God" to Pharaoh (Exodus 7:1), and Isaiah 9:6 calls the coming king "Mighty God"; (b) as an Elohistic replacement for the name (see 42:1); (c) as a real address to a divine king, which Christians find fulfilled in Christ.

Reading 2: "Your throne is (the throne) of God." With a word understood, as in 1 Chronicles 29:23, where "Solomon sat on the LORD's throne," the line means the king's throne is God's. The RSV ("Your divine throne") and NJPS ("Your divine throne is everlasting") follow this reading, and some medieval Jewish commentators explained it so. Reading 3: "Your throne is God," that is, God is its support. Reading 4: emendation. Some scholars propose that elohim replaced an original yihyeh, "will be" ("your throne will be forever"). There is no manuscript support for it.

Hebrews 1:8–9. The author quotes the Greek as one of seven texts showing the Son's superiority to angels. Most commentators (Attridge, Lane, Koester, Harris) take ho theos as vocative: God says to the Son, "Your throne, O God." In 1:9 "God, your God, has anointed you" may likewise be read "O God, your God has anointed you." For Hebrews the psalm addresses the Son both as God and as one anointed by God, a pairing that later fed the church's teaching on the Trinity. Jewish interpreters answer that the psalm addresses a human king, that elohim can mean a ruler, and that the next line, where "God, your God" anoints him, shows he is not God himself. Both readings are honest readings of a line that is open in Hebrew.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a poet borrowing the temple's language
deep.b: This is my own suggestion, not an established view. The poet calls his song "my work" (45:1) and speaks to the king in phrases elsewhere used of God: splendor and majesty (45:3; 96:6; 104:1), a throne "for ever and ever" (45:6; 10:16), a scepter of justice, the love of righteousness (45:7; 11:7). I suspect a Korahite temple singer, trained in hymns to God, was asked to compose for a royal wedding and used the only high language he knew, the language of the temple. That would explain why the address "O God" sits so naturally in the line without implying a theory of the king's divinity, and also why later readers found it easy to hear the Messiah, and Christians the divine Son, in it. Close to this are Mowinckel's and Kraus's discussions of the "court style" of royal psalms.

echoes: Hebrews 1:8–9; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; 1 Kings 3:1; 1 Kings 16:31; Isaiah 9:6–7; Isaiah 61:1–3; Song of Songs 3:6–11; Ephesians 5:25–32; Revelation 19:7; Revelation 21:2

settings.what: A wedding song for a king
settings.by: a court poet, presented as a singer of the Korahite guild (45:0–1)
settings.to: the king (45:2–9, 45:16–17) and the bride (45:10–15), before the wedding guests
settings.when: at a royal wedding, as the bride, perhaps a princess from Tyre, is led into the palace
settings.why: to praise the king as the ideal ruler blessed by God, to call him to rule with justice, and to welcome the foreign bride and urge her to give her loyalty to her new husband and land. Once the first occasion is clear, the extravagant praise reads as court style addressed to God's anointed.
settings.readers: After the exile, with no king on the throne, the psalm became a song of the king to come: the Messiah of the Targum, and the Son of Hebrews 1.
views: Solomon's marriage to Pharaoh's daughter or another princess (traditional).
Ahab and Jezebel, or another king of Israel, given Tyre and the ivory palaces.
Some conservative interpreters think the poet looked beyond any present king to the Messiah (Delitzsch).

traditions.q: Is the queen of Psalm 45 a picture of Mary?
views: Yes, in a secondary, spiritual sense: the Church applies the queen at the king's right hand to Mary, Queen of Heaven, in the liturgy of her feasts, and Pius XII cited the psalm among texts the theologians applied to her Assumption (Munificentissimus Deus 26, citing Psalm 44:10–14 in the Greek and Latin numbering).

Yes: at feasts of the Theotokos the prokeimenon is Greek Psalm 44:18 (English 45:17) with the verse 44:11 (English 45:10, "Listen, daughter"), the Entrance into the Temple also uses Greek 44:13–15 (English 45:12–14), and the "queen in gold of Ophir" is a common image of Mary in hymns and icons.
The bride and queen are usually read as the church, the bride of Christ; Lutherans honor Mary as the mother of God but do not make the queen of this psalm a teaching about her.
The queen is the church gathered from the nations (45:10–12), as Calvin explained; applying the verse to Mary is not the psalm's meaning.

Most read the bride as the church, the people of God, and the psalm as a type of Christ's marriage to his people (Revelation 19:7); a Marian reading is rejected. Spurgeon's Treasury of David reads the bride as the church.

title: A Mighty Fortress
sum: Psalm 46 (Greek 45) is a song of trust in God's protection of his city. Even if the earth gives way and the mountains slide into the sea, "we will have no fear." Against the raging waters stands a gentle river that gladdens the city of God; against the raging nations stands God's voice, which melts the earth. The refrain says it twice: "The LORD of Armies is with us; / the God of Jacob is a high fort for us."

The last stanza invites the world to come and see what God has done: he ends wars, breaks bows and spears, burns weapons. Then God speaks: "Let go, and know that I am God." Martin Luther's "A mighty fortress is our God" is built on this psalm.

views.H: Titled "Of the sons of Korah." Many traditional and some modern readers connect it with the deliverance of Jerusalem from Sennacherib in 701 BC (2 Kings 19:35).
views.C: One of the "Songs of Zion" (46, 48, 76, 84, 87, 122), probably sung at a temple festival. It draws on old images of God's victory over the sea and the nations, and on the belief that Zion could not fall, a belief Jeremiah later warned against trusting blindly (Jeremiah 7:4).
views.L: Luther's hymn made it the Reformation's psalm. It is widely read at times of national crisis.
views.J: Radak and others read the final stanza of the wars of Gog and Magog in the messianic age (Ezekiel 38–39).
views.X: The river of 46:4 is read of the Holy Spirit and of the river of life (John 7:38; Revelation 22:1); "God with us" (46:7) points to Immanuel (Matthew 1:23). 46:10 is often used as a call to contemplative prayer.

echoes: 2 Kings 19:35; Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah 8:8–10; Isaiah 17:12–14; Isaiah 2:4; Ezekiel 47:1–12; Joel 3:18; Zechariah 14:8; Revelation 22:1; Matthew 1:23; Psalm 48:1–14; Psalm 76:1–12
links: A Mighty Fortress Is Our God
A Mighty Fortress Is Our God

settings.what: A Song of Zion: trust in God's protection of Jerusalem
settings.by: the congregation, led by the Korahite singers ("us")
settings.to: the congregation and the nations (46:8, 46:10); God himself speaks in 46:10
settings.when: probably at a temple festival celebrating God as protector of Zion; some think after a deliverance such as 701 BC
settings.why: to build confidence that God's presence makes his city safe even if the world collapses, and to summon the nations to stop their wars and acknowledge him. Knowing it was sung in Jerusalem shows why the river and the city matter: the safety is God's presence in the temple, not walls.
settings.readers: For Jews after the exile, whose city had in fact fallen, the psalm became a hope for God's final reign, when wars will end, and a reminder that the true refuge is God himself.

title: God Has Gone Up with a Shout
sum: Psalm 47 (Greek 46) calls all the peoples to clap and shout for God, the great King over the whole earth. He subdued nations under Israel and chose its land; now he "has gone up" with shouting and the ram's horn, and takes his seat on his holy throne. The song ends with a remarkable scene: the nobles of the nations gather, "the people of the God of Abraham."

It is one of the enthronement psalms that proclaim "God rules as King" (47, 93, 95–99). Christians sing it on Ascension Day; Jews recite it seven times before the ram's horn is blown on Rosh Hashanah.

views.H: Titled "Of the sons of Korah." Some traditional readers linked it with David bringing the ark to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:15) or with a victory.
views.C: An enthronement psalm. Mowinckel proposed a yearly autumn festival at which God's kingship was celebrated with a procession of the ark into the temple; others see the psalm as a hymn to God's universal kingship without a specific ritual. Its openness to the nations (47:9) is often compared with Isaiah 2:2–4.
views.L: Sung on Ascension Day in the Western and Eastern churches since early times. In the synagogue it is recited seven times before the shofar is sounded on Rosh Hashanah.
views.J: Read on Rosh Hashanah, the day the Jewish liturgy celebrates God as King of the world (the Malkhuyot verses). The rabbis read "God has gone up with a shout" of God rising from the throne of justice to the throne of mercy when Israel blows the shofar (Leviticus Rabbah 29:3).
views.X: Augustine and the liturgy read 47:5 of Christ's ascension (Acts 1:9–11). The gathering of the nations as Abraham's people (47:9) was read of Gentiles joining the church (Galatians 3:7–9).

echoes: 2 Samuel 6:15; 2 Kings 11:12; Psalm 93:1; Psalm 96:10; Psalm 97:1; Psalm 99:1; Isaiah 2:2–4; Zechariah 14:9; Acts 1:9–11; Galatians 3:7–9; Genesis 12:3

settings.what: A hymn to God as King of all the earth
settings.by: the Korahite singers and the congregation
settings.when: probably at a festival procession in the temple, with the ram's horn, celebrating God's kingship
settings.why: to call every nation to acclaim Israel's God as their King and to celebrate his taking his throne. Knowing it was sung in Jerusalem gives its universal call its force: a small nation summoning the world to its God.
settings.readers: For Jews under Persian and Greek rule, the psalm affirmed that their God, not the emperor, reigned over the nations, and looked to a day when the nations would join Abraham's people.
views: A yearly festival celebrating God's kingship (Mowinckel).
A hymn after a victory or the ark's procession (traditional).
A song of God's coming reign over all nations (Kraus and many recent scholars).

title: The City of the Great King
sum: Psalm 48 (Greek 47) is a hymn to Zion, "the city of our God." Mount Zion is lovely and lofty, the joy of all the earth, given the title of Zaphon, the mountain of the gods. Kings once gathered against it, saw it, panicked and fled, as ships break in an east wind. "What we had heard, we have now seen." In the temple the worshipers ponder God's loyal love.

The psalm ends with a tour: walk around Zion, count its towers, look closely at its walls, so you can tell the next generation "that this is God, our God, for ever and ever." It was the Levites' song for Monday in the temple, as it still is in the synagogue.

views.H: Some traditional readers tied the kings' flight to Jehoshaphat's victory (2 Chronicles 20) or Sennacherib's retreat (2 Kings 19).
views.C: A Song of Zion, close to Psalm 46. It uses the Canaanite image of Zaphon and the motif of the nations' attack on God's city. Its confidence is usually dated before 586 BC; Lamentations 2:15 quotes it bitterly after the fall.
views.L: The "song of the day" for Monday in the temple (Mishnah Tamid 7:4) and in the daily synagogue liturgy. The church sings it on feasts of the dedication of a church and for the heavenly Jerusalem.
views.J: The Talmud explains why it is Monday's psalm: on the second day God divided his works and reigned over them (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 31a). Midrash Tehillim reads "the joy of all the earth" of the temple as the place of atonement.
views.X: Christians read Zion as the church and the heavenly city (Hebrews 12:22; Revelation 21:2), and the walk around the walls as meditation on what God has done. Jesus calls Jerusalem "the great King's city" (Matthew 5:35), echoing 48:2.

echoes: Psalm 46:1–11; Psalm 76:1–12; Isaiah 2:2–3; Isaiah 14:13; Isaiah 33:20; Lamentations 2:15; Matthew 5:35; Hebrews 12:22; Revelation 21:2; 2 Kings 19:35–36

settings.what: A Song of Zion and a pilgrims' walk around the city
settings.to: God (48:9–10) and the pilgrims, who are told to walk around the city (48:12–13)
settings.when: at a festival in Jerusalem, perhaps with a procession around the walls
settings.why: to celebrate God's protection of his city, to remember a deliverance, and to teach pilgrims to read the city itself as a witness to God for their children. Knowing the walk was a real practice makes the towers and walls into a sermon in stone.
settings.readers: After the exile, when the walls were ruined and then rebuilt (Nehemiah 2:17; 12:31–40), the psalm became a hope and a liturgy for a smaller Jerusalem that still trusted God's presence there.

title: You Cannot Take It with You
sum: Psalm 49 (Greek 48) is a wisdom poem addressed to the whole world, rich and poor. The teacher asks why he should fear when wealthy, self-confident people surround him. His answer: no one can buy back a life from death. Wise and foolish die alike and leave their wealth to others; they named lands after themselves, but a human in his splendor "does not stay even a night." Like sheep they are herded into Sheol, with Death for their shepherd.

At the turning point the speaker says, "But God will ransom my life / from the hand of Sheol, for he will take me." The refrain (49:12, 49:20) frames the riddle: a human being without understanding is like the animals that perish.
readings: Read as wisdom about wealth
The poem's plain purpose is to free the poor from fear of the rich and to warn the rich: death levels everyone, and money cannot buy life.
Read as a hope beyond death
49:15 uses the verb "take" of Enoch and Elijah. Many Jews and Christians have found here one of the first clear hopes of life with God after death, a step toward the resurrection hope of Daniel 12:2.

views.H: Titled "Of the sons of Korah." The teacher's voice is not tied to any event.
views.C: A wisdom psalm, probably from the late monarchy or the Persian period, close in thought to Ecclesiastes and Job. Its text is among the most damaged in the Psalter (49:11, 49:14). Scholars divide on whether 49:15 means rescue from early death or hope beyond death.
views.L: In many Jewish communities Psalm 49 is recited in the house of mourning during the seven days of shiva. In the church it is read as a warning against greed, often with Luke 12:16–21.
views.J: Recited in the house of mourning in many communities. Medieval Jewish commentators often read 49:15 of the soul's survival and the world to come.
views.X: Jesus' sayings that no one can give anything in exchange for his life, and that he came to give his life "as a ransom in place of many" (Mark 8:37; Mark 10:45), read as the answer to 49:7–9: what no human can pay, God pays.

echoes: Ecclesiastes 2:14–16; Ecclesiastes 5:15; Job 1:21; Job 21:23–26; Genesis 5:24; 2 Kings 2:3; Psalm 73:24; Daniel 12:2; Mark 8:36–37; Mark 10:45; Luke 12:16–21; 1 Timothy 6:7

settings.what: A wisdom teaching on death and wealth
settings.by: a teacher of wisdom, presented as a Korahite singer who sings his riddle to the lyre (49:4)
settings.to: all peoples, rich and poor (49:1–2), and a listener addressed as "you" (49:16)
settings.when: in a setting of teaching or worship where the poor felt threatened by rich and powerful neighbors (49:5–6)
settings.why: to free the poor from fear and to puncture the confidence of the rich by setting death before both, and to state the speaker's own trust that God will ransom him from Sheol. Knowing the audience includes the rich makes the poem a warning as well as a comfort.
settings.readers: For Jews after the exile, living under foreign wealth and power, the psalm set their worth in God's keeping rather than in property, and fed the growing hope of life beyond death.

title: I Do Not Need Your Bulls
sum: Psalm 50 (Greek 49), the first psalm of Asaph, is a courtroom scene. God comes from Zion in fire and storm, summons heaven and earth as witnesses and calls his covenant people to judgment. To the faithful he says: I do not rebuke you for your sacrifices, but I do not need them; every animal is already mine, and if I were hungry I would not tell you. Offer thanks, keep your vows, call on me in trouble.

To the wicked, who recite his commandments while joining thieves, adulterers and slanderers, he says: you thought I was like you. Understand, or I will tear you apart. The way back is open: the one who offers thanks honors God and will see his rescue.

views.H: Asaph was David's chief singer (1 Chronicles 16:5–7); traditional readers took the psalm as his prophetic word, since Asaph is called a seer in 2 Chronicles 29:30.
views.C: A prophetic liturgy, perhaps from a covenant renewal festival, with God speaking through a temple prophet or singer. Its themes (sacrifice versus obedience, the commandments) are close to Hosea, Micah and Jeremiah 7, and many date it to the eighth or seventh century BC.
views.L: Read in Lent and on days of penitence. Its call to offer thanks lies behind the Christian "sacrifice of praise" in the eucharistic prayers (Hebrews 13:15).
views.J: The rabbis taught that in the age to come all sacrifices will cease except the thank offering (Leviticus Rabbah 9:7). Midrash Tehillim reads the opening three names of God as the three names by which the world was created.
views.X: The church fathers saw here the end of animal sacrifice and the true sacrifice of praise and a changed life (Romans 12:1; Hebrews 13:15–16). Augustine read 50:3 of Christ's second coming.

echoes: Exodus 19:16–18; Exodus 20:2; Exodus 24:5–8; Deuteronomy 32:1; Isaiah 1:2; Isaiah 1:11–17; Micah 6:1–8; Hosea 5:14; Hosea 6:6; Jeremiah 7:9–10; Acts 17:24–25; Hebrews 13:15; Romans 2:21–23

settings.what: A covenant lawsuit in God's own voice
settings.by: God, speaking through a temple singer or prophet of the Asaph guild (the title)
settings.to: Israel gathered for worship: first the faithful who bring sacrifices (50:5–15), then "the wicked" who recite the covenant but break it (50:16–22); heaven and earth are called as witnesses (50:4)
settings.when: at a festival of covenant renewal or a temple service where the commandments were recited
settings.why: to correct two errors: that sacrifice feeds or obliges God, and that reciting the covenant excuses breaking it. The goal is not condemnation but a return to thanksgiving and honest living. Knowing the hearers were worshipers, not pagans, makes the rebuke a warning to the religious.
settings.readers: After the exile, when the rebuilt temple's sacrifices resumed, the psalm kept alive the prophets' teaching that God wants thanks and obedience above offerings; after AD 70 it helped Judaism understand prayer and thanks as offerings.

title: Create a Pure Heart in Me
sum: Psalm 51 (Greek 50), the Miserere, is the Bible's great prayer of repentance. Its title sets it after Nathan confronted David over Bathsheba and Uriah. The speaker throws himself on God's grace and loyal love, names his rebellion, guilt and sin, and asks to be wiped clean, washed, purified with hyssop and made whiter than snow. He admits that God is right to judge, that he was born in guilt, and that God wants faithfulness deep inside.

Then he asks for more than pardon: a new heart, created by God, a steady spirit, not to lose God's holy spirit, the joy of salvation back, and a willing spirit. He promises to teach sinners and to praise God, because the sacrifice God wants is a broken spirit. The last two verses pray for Zion's walls and for sacrifices that please God.
readings: Read with the title

As David's confession after 2 Samuel 12, the psalm shows a king, guilty of adultery and murder, for which the law provided no sacrifice, asking God for what only God can give. "Against you alone" and "bloodguilt" take on sharp meaning.
Read as the community's prayer

Without the title, especially with 51:18–19, the psalm is the prayer of any sinner, and of Israel in exile, confessing sin and asking God to rebuild Jerusalem. Most scholars think the poem was used this way, whatever its origin.

views.H: David's own prayer after Nathan's visit (2 Samuel 12:1–14). Defenders of the title point to the personal tone, "bloodguilt" (51:14) and the lack of a sacrifice for his sins (51:16); they read 51:18–19 as a prayer for Jerusalem's walls, which David and Solomon were building.
views.C: An individual lament and confession, linked to David by editors. 51:18–19 is widely judged a later addition from the exile or the early Persian period. The language is close to Ezekiel (new heart and spirit, Ezekiel 36:25–27) and Isaiah 40–66 ("holy spirit," Isaiah 63:10–11), suggesting an exilic date for the whole to some scholars.
views.L: The most-used penitential psalm in Christian worship: the fourth of the seven penitential psalms, sung at Lauds on Fridays, on Ash Wednesday (the Anglican Commination) and in Lent; Allegri's Miserere was sung in the Sistine Chapel in Holy Week. 51:7 accompanies the Asperges, the sprinkling with holy water. 51:15 opens the Liturgy of the Hours; in the Orthodox Church Psalm 50 (Greek) is read in nearly every service.
views.J: 51:15 is said before every Amidah (Bavli Berakhot 4b). The Talmud says David's sin happened to teach the power of repentance to individuals (Bavli Avodah Zarah 4b–5a), and teaches that the humble heart counts as all the sacrifices (Bavli Sanhedrin 43b). Some rabbis minimized David's guilt (Bavli Shabbat 56a); others used 51:5 for the inclination to sin present from birth.
views.X: Augustine made 51:5 a chief Old Testament text for original sin. Luther called it the psalm that teaches the true knowledge of sin and grace. 51:4 is quoted in Romans 3:4. The prayer for a clean heart and the holy spirit shaped Christian teaching on regeneration and the Spirit.

deep.b: Readers sometimes object that 51:4 ignores Bathsheba and Uriah. Three things can be said. First, the Old Testament has no doubt that David wronged them: Nathan's parable is about a poor man robbed (2 Samuel 12:1–6), and David is punished (2 Samuel 12:10–14). Second, the psalm speaks in the language of God's law court: God is the judge whose word condemned David (2 Samuel 12:9, "Why have you despised the word of the LORD?"), and so the one before whom he must confess. Third, the next lines explain the purpose: "So you are in the right when you speak." David accepts God's verdict without excuse. Joseph's refusal in Genesis 39:9 shows the same logic: a wrong against a person is first a sin against God. Many modern readers still find the line uncomfortable, and that discomfort is part of reading it honestly.

51:16–17 says God does not want sacrifice; 51:19 looks forward to sacrifices that please him. Three explanations are common. (1) The law had no sacrifice for David's sins, so he offers his broken spirit; once forgiven, the community can offer again (traditional). (2) The prophets' contrast is not a rejection of sacrifice but of sacrifice without obedience, as in 1 Samuel 15:22 and 50:8–15; 51:19's "sacrifices offered rightly" are those of a renewed heart (Calvin, Kidner). (3) 51:18–19 was added by a later hand, when the temple lay in ruins, to correct or complete 51:16–17 (many critical scholars). Jewish tradition after AD 70 read 51:17 as permission to offer prayer and repentance in place of sacrifice (Bavli Sanhedrin 43b; compare Hosea 14:2).

deep.title: Claude's theory: the psalm moves through the temple
deep.b: This is my own reading, offered as a theory. The verbs of cleansing follow the order of a person being restored to the temple: wiping and washing (51:1–2), as for impurity; hyssop (51:7), the priest's sprinkler at the end of a purification rite (Leviticus 14:4–7; Numbers 19:18); then hearing "joy and celebration" (51:8), the sound of the festival crowd; then the altar (51:19). The speaker, barred from God's presence (51:11), asks God himself to act as the priest at each step, and at the end imagines the altar in use again. If so, Psalm 51 is not anti-ritual but a prayer that God perform the ritual inwardly where no rite could reach. This overlaps with Milgrom's work on purification and with commentators who note the priestly vocabulary (Tate, Hossfeld and Zenger), but the step-by-step mapping is mine.

echoes: 2 Samuel 11:1–12:25; Exodus 34:6–7; Leviticus 14:4–7; Numbers 19:18; Isaiah 1:16–18; Ezekiel 36:25–27; Jeremiah 31:33; Isaiah 63:10–11; Romans 3:4; Romans 5:12; Luke 18:13; Psalm 32:1–5; Psalm 50:14–23

settings.what: A prayer of confession and renewal
settings.by: a sinner who knows his guilt; the title says David, after Nathan's rebuke
settings.to: God; with a promise to teach other sinners (51:13)
settings.when: after the sin is exposed (the title: 2 Samuel 12), at a time when sacrifice cannot help (51:16); 51:18–19 assumes Jerusalem's walls need building
settings.why: to confess without excuse, to appeal to God's own character for mercy, and to ask for a new heart and spirit, not only pardon. Reading it with the title shows a king who could not be tried by any court placing himself under God's judgment.
settings.readers: After the exile, Israel prayed the psalm as its own confession: the community that had sinned and lost its temple asked God to cleanse it and rebuild Zion's walls (51:18), as Nehemiah later did.
views: The title is historical; 51:18–19 fits David's building of Jerusalem (traditional; Kidner).
David's prayer adapted for the exiles by 51:18–19 (many scholars).
The whole psalm comes from the exile, and the title is an early interpretation (Hossfeld and Zenger).

traditions.q: Does Psalm 51:5 teach that every person is born guilty of original sin?
views: Every human inherits original sin, a deprivation of original holiness and justice, transmitted by propagation, not imitation; it is called sin in an analogical sense, not a personal fault (Catechism 404–405; Trent, Session 5). Psalm 51:5 is read as expressing this state.

Humans inherit the ancestral sin's consequences, mortality and a weakened nature inclined to sin, but not Adam's personal guilt. The verse confesses that one is born into a fallen world; many fathers read it of the corruption of human nature, not of inherited guilt.
Yes: original sin is true sin that condemns, a lack of fear and trust in God and an inborn concupiscence; the Formula of Concord cites this verse.
Yes: from conception every person bears Adam's guilt and a corrupt nature (Westminster Confession 6.3, citing Psalm 51:5).
Yes, humans are born with a corrupt nature (Article 7), but prevenient grace is given to all and removes the guilt that would condemn infants; Wesley defended original sin using this verse.
No inherited guilt: children are innocent until they sin themselves; the verse describes the sinful world and the speaker's own sinfulness in poetic language, not a doctrine of guilt at birth.

traditions.q: Can a believer lose the Holy Spirit (51:11)?
views: No: the Spirit, once given, is never taken from the elect (Westminster Confession 17). David prayed for the restoration of joy and assurance, or for his royal anointing, not against final loss of salvation.
Most hold that the indwelling Spirit is the believer's permanent seal (Ephesians 1:13–14; John 14:16), so a Christian need not pray this prayer as David did under the old covenant.

Yes: grievous (mortal) sin drives out sanctifying grace and the indwelling of the Spirit, which can be restored through repentance and the sacrament of penance; the psalm is the model prayer of the penitent.
Yes: believers can fall from grace and grieve away the Spirit, and can be restored by repentance (Articles of Religion 12); Wesley read David as a warning and an encouragement.
Yes: believers can fall from faith and lose the Holy Spirit through deliberate sin, and be restored by repentance (Smalcald Articles III.3).

title: The Razor Tongue and the Olive Tree
sum: Psalm 52 (Greek 51) is titled for the moment when Doeg the Edomite told Saul that David had visited the priest Ahimelech, which led to the massacre of the priests of Nob (1 Samuel 22). The psalm speaks to a powerful man who boasts of evil, whose tongue is a sharp razor, who loves lies and devouring words. God will tear him down and uproot him; the righteous will see and laugh: look at the man who trusted his wealth instead of God.
Against him the speaker stands like a leafy olive tree in God's house, trusting God's loyal love forever, waiting on God's good name among his faithful ones.

views.H: The title places it at 1 Samuel 21–22. Doeg's lie by half-truth (he told only what would condemn Ahimelech) and his wealth as Saul's chief herdsman fit 52:1–7.
views.C: A prophetic judgment speech against a powerful liar, combined with a song of trust; probably not originally about Doeg, but linked to him by editors who saw a fit with the betrayal by words.
views.L: Used in Christian prayer against slander and the abuse of power.
views.J: The Mishnah names Doeg among those with no share in the world to come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2); the Talmud presents him as a great Torah scholar whose learning was only on his lips (Bavli Sanhedrin 106b). The rabbis took the psalm as a lesson on the deadliness of lashon hara, evil speech.
views.X: Augustine read Doeg (whose name he took to mean "movement") as the earthly-minded and the olive tree as the church rooted in God's mercy. The psalm is often used in teaching on the tongue (James 3).

echoes: 1 Samuel 21:1–9; 1 Samuel 22:6–23; Psalm 120:2–4; Psalm 92:12–14; Jeremiah 11:16; Proverbs 6:16–19; James 3:5–8; Romans 11:17–24

settings.what: A judgment on a powerful liar, and a song of trust
settings.by: the title: David, when he learned of Doeg's report; otherwise a faithful worshiper
settings.to: the "hero" himself (52:1–5), then the righteous (52:6–7), then God (52:9)
settings.when: after a betrayal by words that led to bloodshed (the title: 1 Samuel 22)
settings.why: to expose the liar's power as hollow, to announce God's judgment on him, and to declare trust in God's loyal love instead of wealth. Knowing the title's story, the "razor tongue" is not an exaggeration: Doeg's words killed a town.
settings.readers: For the community after the exile, often harmed by powerful informers and officials, the psalm promised that God uproots those who trust in wealth and lies, and roots the faithful in his house.

title: The Fool Says There Is No God
sum: Psalm 53 (Greek 52) is the second copy in the Psalter of the poem we know as Psalm 14. The fool says to himself, "There is no God"; humans have gone rotten; God looks down from heaven and finds no one who does good, not one. The evildoers eat up God's people as they eat bread and never call on God.

The two copies differ in small ways throughout and in a large way in 53:5, where Psalm 53 describes an enemy army scattered and its bones left unburied. Most strikingly, Psalm 53 has "God" wherever Psalm 14 has "the LORD": the clearest evidence of the editing of the Elohistic Psalter.

views.H: Both copies are titled "of David." Traditional readers explain the doubling as David's reuse of his own psalm for a new occasion, perhaps a military victory (53:5).
views.C: Psalm 53 is the Elohistic edition of Psalm 14 (or both go back to a common original). The rewritten 53:5 may reflect a later event, such as the retreat of Sennacherib's army, or may have grown from a damaged text of 14:5–6.
views.L: Psalm 14 is the more used of the two in worship; Psalm 53 is known mainly through Paul's use of the poem in Romans 3.
views.J: Rashi reads Psalm 14 of Nebuchadnezzar destroying the first temple and Psalm 53 of Titus destroying the second; the doubling showed Jewish readers that history repeats its pattern of arrogance and fall.
views.X: Romans 3:10–12 quotes the poem to show that all, Jews and Gentiles, are under sin and need God's righteousness through faith. Augustine and the Reformers read it as a description of fallen humanity.

deep.b:
The site's Plain English Translation of Psalm 53 follows its Psalm 14 wherever the Hebrew is the same, so the differences can be seen at a glance. They are:

  • Title (53:0; 14:0): Psalm 53 adds "On mahalath" and "a maskil" to "For the music director... of David."
  • 53:1 (14:1): "and" added between the verbs, and 'avel, "injustice," for 'alilah, "deeds." Psalm 14 has "what they do is detestable"; Psalm 53 has "their injustice is detestable."
  • 53:2 (14:2): "God" for "the LORD."
  • 53:3 (14:3): kullo sag, "every one has slid back," for hakkol sar, "every one has strayed."
  • 53:4 (14:4): no "all" before "those who do wrong"; "God" for "the LORD."
  • 53:5 (14:5–6): Psalm 14 has two verses: God is with the righteous generation, and the LORD is the refuge of the poor whose plans are mocked. Psalm 53 has one longer verse: "where no dread had been. / For God has scattered the bones of your besieger. / You have put them to shame, because God has thrown them away." Many of the Hebrew letters are similar, so one version may have been read or rewritten from the other.
  • 53:6 (14:7): plural "rescues" for the singular, and "God" for "the LORD."

Where Psalm 14 has "the LORD" (YHWH) in 14:2, 14:4 and 14:7, Psalm 53 has "God"; the fourth "LORD" (14:6) falls in the rewritten verse, which names God twice. Psalm 14 already had "God" in three places, which Psalm 53 keeps. This pattern is the main evidence that an editor deliberately replaced the name in Psalms 42–83 (see the topic on the Elohistic Psalter). The Greek copies (Psalms 13 and 52 in Greek numbering) differ too: many Greek manuscripts of Psalm 13 add after 14:3 the string of verses that Paul quotes in Romans 3:13–18, probably borrowed from Romans; Psalm 52 Greek lacks it.

echoes: Psalm 14:1–7; Romans 3:9–12; Genesis 6:5–12; Genesis 11:5; 1 Samuel 25:25; Psalm 10:4; Micah 3:2–3; Jeremiah 8:1–2; Job 42:10

settings.what: A prophetic lament over human corruption
settings.by: a prophet-like singer (the title: David), speaking about the fool and, in 53:4, quoting God ("my people")
settings.to: the congregation, with words aimed at the oppressors (53:5) and a closing prayer for Israel (53:6)
settings.when: in a time when powerful insiders exploited the poor; 53:5 adds the memory of an enemy army destroyed
settings.why: to expose practical atheism as the root of injustice, to assure the oppressed that God sees and acts, and to pray for Israel's restoration. In this second copy the stress shifts from comfort for the poor (Psalm 14:5–6) to the defeat of an outside enemy.
settings.readers: For the editors of the Elohistic Psalter and the Israelites after the exile who sang it, the psalm in its new form joined the old lament to the hope that God would bring his people back from captivity.

title: Save Me by Your Name
sum: Psalm 54 (Greek 53) is a short prayer for rescue, titled for the time when the people of Ziph twice told Saul where David was hiding (1 Samuel 23:19; 1 Samuel 26:1). The speaker asks God to save him by his name and power: outsiders and brutal men are hunting his life, and they give God no place. Then he states his trust: God is my helper.
He asks God to turn his enemies' evil back on them, and vows a freewill sacrifice and thanks to the LORD's good name, for God has rescued him from every distress.

views.H: The title quotes 1 Samuel 23:19 almost exactly. David was betrayed by people of his own tribe, which gives "outsiders" (54:3) the sense of people who acted like strangers.
views.C: An individual lament of a common pattern (plea, complaint, trust, vow). The title was probably added by an editor who matched it to the Ziphite story. 54:3 also appears in 86:14 with small changes, showing a common stock of prayer phrases.
views.L: Its opening words in Latin, Deus in nomine tuo, were said daily at Prime in the Roman Breviary for centuries.
views.J: The Midrash on Psalms reflects on the Ziphites' betrayal and on David's refusal to harm Saul (1 Samuel 26). The name of God (54:1, 54:6) is a frequent theme of Jewish prayer.
views.X: Augustine read the outsiders as those who know nothing of God, and the freewill sacrifice as praise offered freely, not by compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).

echoes: 1 Samuel 23:14–29; 1 Samuel 26:1–25; Psalm 86:14; Exodus 3:13–15; Proverbs 18:10; Leviticus 7:16; Psalm 7:15–16; Acts 4:12

settings.what: A prayer for rescue from betrayers
settings.by: a person in danger; the title says David when the Ziphites betrayed him
settings.when: while being hunted by enemies (the title: in the wilderness of Ziph, 1 Samuel 23)
settings.why: to call on God's name and power to save, to state trust in God as helper, and to promise a thank offering after rescue. The title shows that the threat came from neighbors who should have protected him.
settings.readers: For Israelites after the exile, praying in the collected Psalter, the psalm was a model of how to pray when betrayed, moving from plea to confident thanks.

title: If Only I Had Wings
sum: Psalm 55 (Greek 54) is a lament of a person overwhelmed by fear. His heart writhes, terror covers him, and he wishes for a dove's wings to fly away to the wilderness. The city around him is full of violence; strife walks its walls, and harm and deceit fill its square. Worst of all, the attacker is not an enemy but a close friend, a man of his own rank, with whom he once walked to the house of God.

He prays that the traitors go down to Sheol alive, then turns to trust: he calls on God evening, morning and noon, and God hears. The friend's words were smoother than butter but were drawn swords. The psalm ends with advice to others, "Throw your load on the LORD," and a final word: "But I will trust in you."
readings: Read as betrayal
The heart of the psalm is 55:12–14 and 55:20–21: the pain of being betrayed by a friend and fellow worshiper. Jewish tradition thought of Ahithophel; Christians of Judas.
Read as a city's corruption
Others stress 55:9–11: the speaker may be a leader in a Jerusalem torn by factions, perhaps in the last years of the monarchy, praying against conspirators.

views.H: Titled "a maskil of David." Traditional readers placed it during Absalom's revolt, when Ahithophel, David's adviser, joined the plot (2 Samuel 15:12, 31) and David fled the city (2 Samuel 15:14).
views.C: An individual lament with a long complaint. The changes of address (from the friend as "he" to "you" and back) and the difficult Hebrew in 55:18–21 suggest to some that two poems were joined. Proposed dates run from the monarchy to the Persian period.
views.L: Mendelssohn's anthem "Hear my prayer" ("O for the wings of a dove") made 55:1–7 famous in English-speaking churches. 55:22 is one of the most-memorized verses of comfort.
views.J: The Talmud cites 55:17 for praying three times a day (Bavli Berakhot 31a; compare 26b) and 55:23 for the short lives of Doeg and Ahithophel (Bavli Sanhedrin 106b).
views.X: Augustine and later commentators heard Christ's voice in 55:12–14, betrayed by Judas, who had shared his table (John 13:18). 1 Peter 5:7 echoes the Greek of 55:22.

echoes: 2 Samuel 15:12; 2 Samuel 15:31; 2 Samuel 17:23; Psalm 41:9; John 13:18; Matthew 26:47–50; Jeremiah 9:2–8; Genesis 11:7; Numbers 16:33; Daniel 6:10; 1 Peter 5:7; Proverbs 5:3–4

settings.what: A lament over violence in the city and a friend's betrayal
settings.by: a person in danger in the city (the title: David), possibly a leader facing a conspiracy
settings.to: God (55:1–11, 55:15–19, 55:23), the betraying friend (55:13–14) and other believers (55:22)
settings.when: while violence fills the city and a trusted companion leads the attack (55:9–14, 55:20–21)
settings.why: to pour out fear and the longing to escape, to hand the traitors over to God's judgment instead of taking revenge, and to model the turn to trust, so that others will throw their burdens on the LORD. Knowing the betrayer was a close friend and fellow worshiper explains the poem's intensity.
settings.readers: For the post-exilic community, divided by factions and betrayals (Nehemiah 6:10–19), the psalm offered words for being wronged by one's own people and a pattern of daily prayer.
views: David during Absalom's revolt, with Ahithophel as the friend (traditional).
A later king or leader in Jerusalem facing a palace plot (Kraus).
An ordinary worshiper wronged by a friend; the city is the setting of the conflict (Tate).
